To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) superelevation of turbidity currents is enhanced by the runup of currents onto the outer banks, (2) runup is a function of the balance of kinetic and potential energy, and (3) the first bend in the channel serves as a filter for excess discharge.
the interaction between a turbidity current and topography in a sinuous submarine channel causes the current to superelevate at bend apexes and runup onto the outer bank.

the superelevation of turbidity currents at bend apexes was 85–142% greater that the value predicted by balance of centrifugal pressure-gradient forces and that runup of turbidity currents onto the outer bank of bends caused deposition of coarse particles onto levee crests.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interactions between turbidity currents, sedimentation, and channel geometry.
the interaction of turbidity currents and channelized flow in a sinuous channel.
the evolution of a channel form in a sedimentation-dominated environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the channel form is controlled by a balance of the forces acting upon the flow and the sedimentation processes occurring in the channel.
the sinuous channel form is a result of the interplay of flow and sedimentation in a complex, nonlinear feedback loop.
the channelized current was not able to maintain its initial conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interaction between turbidity currents, topography, and sediment transport processes is highly dynamic, with the channel form and flow conditions continually evolving.

sinuous channel planform is controlled by the interaction of the channel with its sediment-laden flow, whereas the cross-sectional geometry is determined by the interaction of flow with the channel bed.
sinuous channel planforms are not self-maintained, but instead evolve to match the properties of the currents that form them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of sinuosity, channel width, and channel relief are strongly influenced by the interaction between turbidity currents, topographic gradients, and sediment deposition.
the evolution of the channel planform and morphology are strongly coupled with the flow properties of the current.

the interaction between turbidity currents flowing in a sinuous channel and topography results in the formation of a complex deposit that is not easily reproduced in a simple, one-dimensional model of turbidity currents.
